Short version: do NOT assume the debt is too old, and DO respond — immediately, today. Your written answer was due Tuesday, September 15, 2026, so you are about two days late, but in Texas a late answer still works as long as it is on file before the court signs a default judgment.

1) Is it too old to sue on? Probably not clearly, and you should not rely on that. Texas gives a debt collector four years from the day the claim accrues to BRING suit, and what counts is the file-stamp date on the petition — here July 14, 2025 — not today's date and not the date you were served (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 16.004(a)). Running your three dates:
  • Last payment March 2021 + 4 years = March 2025 → a July 14, 2025 filing would be LATE.
  • First missed payment April 2021 + 4 years = April 2025 → a July 14, 2025 filing would be LATE.
  • Charge-off / demand for the full balance November 2021 + 4 years = November 2025 → a July 14, 2025 filing is TIMELY.
The rule node says accrual on a revolving account (like a store card) is generally the default/acceleration date — the charge-off and demand — not the last-payment date, which points to the suit being timely. But it also says the accrual date on a revolving account is not settled by a single controlling Texas case and that the first-missed-payment date is a recognized alternative. So limitations is a genuine, arguable defense here, not a sure winner: raise it, don't rely on it.
  One extra point to take to a lawyer: the petition was filed July 14, 2025 but you were not served until September 1, 2026 — about 14 months later. Under Texas law, filing alone only stops the clock if the plaintiff then exercised diligence in getting you served. That delay may be a real timeliness argument even under the November 2021 accrual date. That is a merits question for a licensed attorney, not something this tool decides.
  Also note: because the plaintiff is a debt buyer, Tex. Fin. Code § 392.307(c)-(d) bars a debt buyer from suing after the limitations period at all, and provides that no payment or reaffirmation revives a barred consumer debt.

2) Do you have to respond? Yes — and this is the urgent part. Limitations is an AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE in Texas (Tex. R. Civ. P. 94). Even a completely time-barred debt can turn into a valid judgment against you if you don't answer and say so in writing. Texas justice courts enter default judgments on time-barred debts every day against people who never responded.

3) The dates. Service: Tuesday, September 1, 2026. Justice-court debt claims get 14 days to file a written answer (Tex. R. Civ. P. 502.5). September 1 + 14 days = Tuesday, September 15, 2026 — a business day, so no weekend/holiday extension. Today is September 17, 2026, which is 16 days after service, i.e., 2 days past that date.

4) What that means depends on one fact I don't have: whether the court has already SIGNED a default judgment.
  • If NO default judgment has been signed (most likely, only two days out): file your written answer with the Harris County justice court TODAY. A default judgment cannot be entered while an answer is on file, so a late answer filed before signing defeats the default. Filing an answer is free. In the answer, deny the claim and expressly plead the statute of limitations (and, if the plaintiff is a debt buyer, Tex. Fin. Code § 392.307).
  • If a default judgment HAS been signed: get the exact date it was signed. You then have two short windows — a motion to set aside / new trial within 14 days of signing (Tex. R. Civ. P. 505.3), and an appeal to the county court for a brand-new trial within 21 days of signing (or of denial of that motion) under Tex. R. Civ. P. 506.1(a), perfected by a bond, cash deposit, or a sworn statement of inability to pay. The appeal route needs no excuse for the default. After 21 days both doors close and you would need to see a lawyer about equitable relief.

5) Two more things to check while you file:
  • Venue: you are entitled to be sued in the county AND precinct where you live (or another proper venue under TRCP 502.4(b)). If this JP precinct is not yours, file a sworn motion to transfer venue — due no later than 21 days after your answer is filed (TRCP 502.4(d)); answering first does not waive it.
  • Confirm the citation actually names a justice (JP) court. If it names a county court at law or district court, the deadline is different (TRCP 99(b): 10:00 a.m. on the Monday next after 20 days from service), which would put you at Monday, September 21, 2026 — still open. Read the caption before assuming.
  • Finally, tell your lawyer about any tolling facts (time living outside Texas, military service, unsound mind, fraudulent concealment). Tolling is not encoded in this rule node and can change the limitations math in your favor.

Bottom line: file a written answer with the court today pleading limitations, and confirm with the clerk whether a default judgment has already been signed — that single answer determines whether you use the late-answer route or the 14-day/21-day post-judgment windows.
answer.missing_fact: Whether a default judgment has already been SIGNED in the Harris County justice court case (and, if so, the exact date it was signed) — the answer deadline of September 15, 2026 has passed, so this fact decides whether she files a late answer now or must use the 14-day motion to set aside / 21-day appeal windows. (Secondarily missing and flagged: any tolling facts, and confirmation that the citation names a JP court rather than a county court at law.)

answer.answer:
Short version: nothing is overdue, and your protective deadline is Tuesday, September 29, 2026 — but the exact due date depends on one fact I don't have (the date of the follow-up mailing), so treat Sept. 29 as your working deadline and confirm the real one from the court file.

Why. What happened at your apartment is 'substituted service' under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 415.20(a): the papers were left with a competent adult member of your household (your adult son, who lives with you) and the process server must THEN mail a copy of the summons and complaint by first-class mail to that same address. Under § 415.20(a), service done this way 'is deemed complete on the 10th day after the mailing' — not on the day the papers were handed to your son. Your 30 days to respond (CCP § 412.20(a)(3)) run from the deemed-complete date, not from August 20.

The arithmetic, using the earliest possible mailing date (same day as the drop-off, Aug. 20, 2026):
• Aug. 20, 2026 (mailing) + 10 days = Aug. 30, 2026 → service deemed complete
• Aug. 30, 2026 + 30 days = Sept. 29, 2026 → answer due

That Sept. 29 figure is the EARLIEST your deadline can be. Any later mailing pushes it out day-for-day: mailed Aug. 21 → complete Aug. 31 → due Sept. 30; mailed Aug. 24 → complete Sept. 3 → due Oct. 3. And if the required mailing was never done at all, substituted service was never completed under § 415.20(a) and no 30-day clock has started (in that situation filing an answer would be the wrong first move — see below). Either way, as of today, Sept. 17, 2026, you have at least 12 days left. No deadline has passed and no default can properly be entered yet.

How to pin down the real date: look at the PROOF OF SERVICE in the court's file for your case (the clerk's office or the court's online case portal). The server's proof of substituted service states the date the copy was mailed. Add 10 days to that mailing date, then add 30 days — that is your true due date. Don't wait for the answer to that question, though; work to the Sept. 29 floor.

Three things that decide whether a timely answer actually protects you:
1) The filing fee. A limited-civil answer is rejected by the clerk unless it comes with the first-appearance fee or a fee-waiver application (form FW-001) filed at the same time. A rejected answer does not stop a default. If money is tight, prepare FW-001 now and file it with the answer. (Fee statutes named in the node — Gov. Code §§ 70611, 70613, 68631 — as a flag, not a verified quotation.)
2) Your affirmative defenses. Filing on time is necessary but not sufficient. Under CCP § 431.30(b)(2), an affirmative defense you don't plead is waived. On the Judicial Council answer form (PLD-050) use the affirmative-defenses section and plead, as the facts allow: statute of limitations (CCP § 337 for written contracts / § 339), lack of standing / failure to prove the assignment if a debt buyer is suing, payment, failure to state a cause of action, and identity theft if applicable. A timely bare general denial on a time-barred card debt is a timely surrender. Have someone review the limitations dates with you — when your last payment was made matters.
3) Other timely responses exist. A demurrer (CCP § 430.10) or motion to strike (§§ 435–436) filed within the response period is itself a timely response and stops the default clock; if a demurrer is overruled, the answer is then due on the court's schedule or within 10 days after notice of the ruling (CCP § 472a(b)).

About challenging service: you say the address is your home and the papers went to your adult son who lives there, so the § 415.20 method looks appropriate on its face, and a motion to quash (CCP § 418.10) doesn't appear to fit. But note the trap in the other direction: if you ever did want to contest service or jurisdiction, filing an answer first is a general appearance that waives that objection entirely (CCP § 418.10(e)(3)). So if you learn from the court file that the required mailing was never made, talk to a lawyer or legal-aid attorney about a § 418.10 motion BEFORE you file an answer.

If a deadline is ever missed: an answer filed at any time before the clerk actually ENTERS default is accepted and defeats the default request (CCP § 585(a)); after entry, CCP § 473(b) allows relief for mistake, inadvertence, surprise or excusable neglect if sought within a reasonable time and in no event more than six months.

Check the proof of service in the court file.

answer.answer:
Your last day is Wednesday, October 14, 2026 — and because that date depends on an assumption the collector is allowed to make, the safest course is to mail (and get proof of mailing for) your written dispute well before then, ideally this week.

Here is the arithmetic, step by step, under 12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(b)(5):

1) The collection agency 'provided' the validation information on Friday, September 4, 2026 (the first letter, which was itself the validation notice — so the timing rule in § 1692g(a)/§ 1006.34(a)(1) was met, since the information was in the initial communication).

2) The collector may assume you received it 5 days later, counting ONLY days that are not a Saturday, Sunday, or federal legal holiday:
   - Sat Sept 5 — skipped
   - Sun Sept 6 — skipped
   - Mon Sept 7 — Labor Day, federal holiday — skipped
   - Tue Sept 8 = day 1
   - Wed Sept 9 = day 2
   - Thu Sept 10 = day 3
   - Fri Sept 11 = day 4
   - Sat Sept 12 / Sun Sept 13 — skipped
   - Mon Sept 14 = day 5
   So the assumed receipt date is Monday, September 14, 2026.

3) The 30-day dispute window then runs in ordinary CALENDAR days from that date — no further weekend or holiday exclusions (this is the point the rule flags as critical: the weekend/holiday exclusion applies only to the 5-day receipt assumption, not to the 30 days). September 14 + 16 days = September 30; the remaining 14 days = October 14. So the window ends Wednesday, October 14, 2026.

Today is September 17, 2026, so your window is open with 27 days left.

What a timely written dispute does: under 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(b), if you notify the collector IN WRITING within the 30-day period that you dispute the debt (or any part of it), the collector must cease collection of the disputed portion until it obtains verification (or a copy of a judgment) and mails a copy to you. Two practical points from the same provision:
- A phone dispute does NOT trigger the stop-collection duty — it must be in writing. (An oral dispute is not worthless: under § 1692e(8), reporting the account to a credit bureau without noting that it is disputed can itself be a violation.)
- There is a second, independent trigger: a written request within the same window for the name and address of the ORIGINAL creditor also requires the collector to stop collecting until it mails you that information. Putting both in one letter gives you two independent grounds.

Two caveats worth knowing:
- Because you lost the page that stated the deadline, I can't confirm what end date the notice itself disclosed, or whether the notice contained all the content § 1006.34(c) requires (collector name/address for disputes, your name/address, current creditor, itemization date and amounts, current amount, the dispute-consequence statements). October 14 is the date computed from the mailing date under the regulation; if the notice stated a different (later) date, that is a fact worth checking. Mailing early avoids the issue entirely. A notice missing required content is itself a potential independent § 1692g violation, which is a separate question from your dispute rights — that would be for a consumer-rights attorney to evaluate.
- I've assumed this agency is a covered 'debt collector' under 15 U.S.C. § 1692a(6) — a third-party agency collecting another's defaulted medical bill normally is. If it had somehow acquired the account before it was in default, the validation-notice duties in this rule would not apply to it.

How to do it: send a short signed letter stating that you dispute the debt in its entirety and that you request the name and address of the original creditor; send it to the address the notice gives for disputes; use certified mail with return receipt (or another method that proves the mailing date), and keep a copy. If the collector keeps collecting after receiving it and before mailing you verification, that is a potential § 1692g(b) violation worth documenting.

answer.answer:
Short answer: No. A private debt buyer with an ordinary credit-card judgment cannot garnish your current Texas wages, and the "25% like the federal rules allow" line is wrong as applied to you.

Why, step by step through the facts the rule requires:

1. What is being targeted? Your paycheck — current wages. Tex. Const. art. XVI, § 28 says "No current wages for personal service shall ever be subject to garnishment, except for the enforcement of court-ordered: (1) child support payments; or (2) spousal maintenance." Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 63.004 repeats this and adds that the garnishee (your employer) "shall be discharged from the garnishment as to any debt to the defendant for current wages." Your debt is credit-card debt — not child support and not spousal maintenance — so neither exception applies, and the 50%/support-cap rules (Tex. Fam. Code § 158.009) are irrelevant here.

2. Is the garnishing party a federal agency or program? No — it is a private debt buyer on a state-court judgment. This matters a lot. The "except as otherwise provided by ... federal law" carve-out in § 63.004 is what lets IRS levies (26 U.S.C. § 6331), Department of Education administrative wage garnishment on defaulted federal student loans (20 U.S.C. § 1095a), and federal criminal restitution reach Texas wages. The federal Consumer Credit Protection Act's 25% cap is a *ceiling* on garnishments that are otherwise allowed by the governing law — it is not an independent grant of authority to a private creditor, and it does not override the Texas constitutional bar. On your facts (private debt buyer, no federal debt), the exception does not apply.

3. Are these genuinely "current wages for personal service"? Yes — you are a W-2 employee being paid a paycheck by your employer. This is the core case the protection covers (the harder classification questions involve 1099/business receivables, which is not your situation).

4. Is the writ being served on an out-of-state employer? No — your employer is a Dallas company and you are a Texas resident, so the unsettled conflict-of-laws issue about out-of-state garnishees does not arise.

So if this creditor actually serves a writ of garnishment on your Dallas employer for your paycheck, that garnishment is barred, and your employer should be discharged as to current wages. You (or counsel) should object/respond citing Tex. Const. art. XVI, § 28 and Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 63.004. There is no deadline attached to this protection itself, but if you are ever *served* with garnishment papers, respond promptly — deadlines in the garnishment suit itself are real.

Three things to know so you are not caught off guard (these are separate mechanisms, not wage garnishment):

• Your bank account is a different story. Once your paycheck is deposited, a judgment creditor can generally garnish the bank account. Texas courts are split on whether deposited wages keep their protected character for a short window after deposit, so that argument exists but is not a guarantee. If the account also holds directly deposited Social Security/SSDI or VA benefits, those stay protected after deposit and the bank must automatically shield two months' worth without you asking (42 U.S.C. § 407(a); 31 C.F.R. § 212.6, § 212.3). Texas unemployment benefits (Tex. Lab. Code § 207.075(b)-(c)), workers' compensation (§ 408.201), and retirement benefits (Tex. Prop. Code § 42.0021) also remain exempt — but, unlike the federal automatic protection, those Texas exemptions are not self-executing: you must assert them in the garnishment proceeding (e.g., by answer/claim under TRCP 664a).

• A turnover order is also different. Because wage garnishment is barred, the usual Texas post-judgment tool is a turnover order/receivership under Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 31.002. Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 31.0025(a) bars a court from ordering turnover of wages "before a judgment debtor is paid wages," so such an order cannot reach money still in your employer's hands — but once wages are actually paid to you, a turnover order reaching those proceeds is generally valid and enforceable by contempt. If you ever receive one, the remedy is an exemption objection or an appeal, not ignoring it.

• Deductions your employer itself makes (repaying an advance, unreturned equipment) or deductions you signed a written authorization for are not garnishment at all; they are governed by Tex. Lab. Code § 61.018 and the Texas Workforce Commission wage-claim process.

Bottom line: tell the creditor's lawyer, in writing, that Texas constitutionally prohibits garnishment of current wages for an ordinary consumer-debt judgment and that his 25% CCPA figure has no application to a private judgment against a Texas wage earner. Consider consulting a Texas consumer attorney about protecting your deposit account, since that is where this creditor's realistic options lie.

answer.answer:
Short answer on the merits: I can't tell you whether the judge will throw the judgment out. Under Texas law that decision is a genuinely discretionary, multi-factor judicial call, and this system does not predict how a specific judge will rule. What I can give you is the hard deadline, the test the judge will apply, and your next steps.

THE HARD DEADLINE (this is the urgent part). Your case was in a Dallas County court at law — a county court, not a justice court — so Tex. R. Civ. P. 329b(a) governs: a motion for new trial must be filed on or before the 30th day after the judgment was signed.
• Judgment signed: Tuesday, August 25, 2026.
• August 25 + 30 days = September 24, 2026 (6 days to reach Aug 31, plus 24 more days = Sept 24).
• Today is September 17, 2026, so you have 7 days left — through Thursday, September 24, 2026.
This gate is absolute: if the motion is not filed by September 24, this path is foreclosed no matter how strong your facts are. Do not wait to gather a perfect defense package before filing — file in time and supplement.

THE TEST THE JUDGE WILL APPLY (Craddock v. Sunshine Bus Lines, 133 S.W.2d 124, 126 (Tex. 1939)). The court sets aside a default and grants a new trial where: (1) your failure to answer was not intentional or the result of conscious indifference, but due to a mistake or accident; (2) the motion sets up a meritorious defense; and (3) granting it will cause no delay or other injury to the plaintiff. You have told me you were hospitalized for three weeks (raw input for factor 1) and that you believe the debt was paid in full in 2023 and you have bank records (raw input for factor 2). I am not going to characterize those facts as satisfying or failing any factor — that weighing is the judge's, and a licensed Texas attorney should assess it against your specific records.

Other deterministic gates I checked, and how they come out on your facts:
• Notice restart (TRCP 306a(4)-(5)): does not help or hurt you — you learned of the judgment two days after signing, which is within 20 days, so your clock still runs from August 25, 2026.
• Service: you say you were properly served, so the Peralta/no-service route (which would drop the meritorious-defense element) is not in play, and the full Craddock test applies.
• Not an eviction case, so the 5-day TRCP 510.9 rule and the 14-day justice-court rule (TRCP 505.3) do not apply to you.

DATES TO CALENDAR AFTER YOU FILE.
• If you file a timely motion and the court signs no written order, it is overruled by operation of law 75 days after the judgment was signed — August 25 + 75 days = Sunday, November 8, 2026. That is a status-check date, not a new filing deadline.
• A timely motion for new trial extends your appellate timetable: notice of appeal is due within 90 days after the judgment was signed — August 25 + 90 days = Monday, November 23, 2026 (with a possible 15-day extension window under Tex. R. App. P. 26.3). Missing that date leaves only extraordinary routes.
• The trial court keeps plenary power for 30 days after the motion is overruled (TRCP 329b(e)) — November 8 + 30 days = Tuesday, December 8, 2026 — so it can still grant relief or modify the judgment up to then. Press for a ruling before that date.
• Backup routes if something goes wrong: because you did not participate in the hearing, a restricted appeal to the court of appeals may be available within six months of the judgment (August 25, 2026 + 6 months = February 25, 2027) if error is apparent on the face of the record — for example, an unsupported unliquidated-damages award or a defective return of service. A bill of review has a four-year outer limit. These are case-law gloss items to raise with counsel, not substitutes for the September 24 deadline.

WHAT TO DO THIS WEEK: (1) get the file-stamped copy of the judgment and the court's file from the Dallas County court at law clerk; (2) pull your hospital records for the three-week admission and the 2023 bank records showing payment; (3) file, or have a lawyer file, a motion for new trial no later than September 24, 2026, with a sworn affidavit describing the hospitalization and attaching the payment proof; (4) contact a licensed Texas consumer-debt attorney or your local legal aid office immediately — Dallas-area legal aid intake can be same-week. Also ask counsel about protecting your bank account and wages while the motion is pending, since a signed judgment can support collection efforts.
citations: Craddock v. Sunshine Bus Lines, Inc., 133 S.W.2d 124, 126 (Tex. 1939)
Peralta v. Heights Medical Center, Inc., 485 U.S. 80 (1988)

answer.answer:
Short answer: on the facts as you've described them, the federal FDCPA / Regulation F "7-in-7" rule does not give you a claim against this bank — but that is only the federal half of the picture, and California has its own statute that may well reach an original creditor. Here is the reasoning.

1) The 7-in-7 rule only applies to a covered 'debt collector.' The Regulation F call-frequency presumption (12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2)(i)-(ii)) and FDCPA § 806(5) (15 U.S.C. § 1692d(5)) apply only to entities that meet the definition of 'debt collector' in 15 U.S.C. § 1692a(6). That gate has to be cleared before the call count matters at all.

2) Your facts land squarely in statutory exclusion (A). Section 1692a(6)(A) excludes 'any officer or employee of a creditor while, in the name of the creditor, collecting debts for such creditor.' You have told me: (a) the callers are the bank's own collections department, staffed by bank employees (not an outside vendor working under the bank's brand — that distinction is the single most important one in this analysis, and you have answered it the way that produces exclusion); (b) they are calling under the bank's own actual name, so the statute's carve-back-in for a creditor using 'any name other than his own which would indicate that a third person is collecting' is not triggered; and (c) the debt has not been sold, so there is no debt buyer and no Henson v. Santander 'principal purpose' question to run. On those facts the bank's in-house department is not a covered debt collector, and the 7-in-7 presumption does not apply to it — even though ten calls in seven days about one card would be presumptively unlawful if a covered collector had made them (10 > 7 for the window of 2026-09-11 through 2026-09-17).

3) So I am not telling you the calls are fine — I am telling you the federal statute you named is the wrong tool for this caller. Two important follow-ups:

   • CALIFORNIA. The corpus expressly notes that California's Rosenthal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, Cal. Civ. Code § 1788 et seq., is reported to define 'debt collector' more broadly than the federal FDCPA and to reach original creditors collecting their own consumer debts — meaning the federal exclusion above would NOT necessarily clear the bank under California law. This corpus has NOT verified or encoded the Rosenthal Act's text (the source fetch failed), so I cannot tell you what it requires or predict an outcome. This is the live question in your case and it should go to a California consumer attorney or to a complaint with the CFPB and the California DFPI. Note the timing flag the corpus does give: the Rosenthal Act's limitations period is cited as one year (Cal. Civ. Code § 1788.30(f)). Counting from the most recent calls (2026-09-11 to 2026-09-17), a one-year period would run to roughly 2027-09-11 through 2027-09-17 — so you have time, but do not sit on it, and have counsel confirm the correct period rather than relying on my arithmetic.

   • PRERECORDED / AUTODIALED CALLS TO A CELL PHONE. If any of these ten calls used a prerecorded or artificial voice (or ringless voicemail) to your cell phone without your consent, that is a separate matter under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, 47 U.S.C. § 227(b)(1)(A)(iii), with statutory damages per call, and it is independent of the FDCPA and of who owns the debt — so the bank-employee exclusion above does not shield it. The TCPA is not encoded in this corpus; you'd need counsel on it. Tell your attorney whether the calls were live agents, recordings, or voicemail drops.

4) Practical step now, regardless of which statute applies: keep the evidence. Write down or screenshot every call — date, time, number dialed, whether you answered, whether a voicemail was left, whether it was a live person or a recording. Get your phone carrier's call log for 2026-09-11 onward. That log is the proof any call-frequency claim, federal or state, depends on.

One caution so you aren't misled: nothing here means you have no claim. It means the specific federal 7-in-7 rule does not apply to a creditor's own employees calling in the creditor's own name. If it turns out that some of these calls were actually placed by an outside firm the bank hired to work delinquent accounts under the bank's brand (common, and not visible from caller ID or letterhead), the federal analysis flips — that vendor is not the bank's officer or employee, it regularly collects debts owed to another, and it would be a covered debt collector with its own 7-call-per-7-day ceiling. If you're not certain who was on the other end, ask the caller directly who their employer is.
citations: 15 U.S.C. § 1692a(6) (definition of 'debt collector'; exclusion (A) for a creditor's officer or employee collecting in the creditor's own name; carve-back-in for use of a name suggesting a third party)
Henson v. Santander Consumer USA Inc., 582 U.S. ___ (2017)
Cal. Civ. Code § 1788 et seq. (Rosenthal Act — flagged in the corpus as not yet verified/encoded); Cal. Civ. Code § 1788.30(f) (one-year period)

answer.answer:
Short answer: what you read online overstates Henson. The company you describe is very likely still covered by the FDCPA — do not assume you have no rights.

Here is the reasoning, step by step through the coverage gate in 15 U.S.C. § 1692a:

1) There are TWO independent ways to be a 'debt collector' under § 1692a(6). Meeting either one is enough: (a) the PRINCIPAL PURPOSE test — any business the principal purpose of which is the collection of any debts; or (b) the REGULARLY-COLLECTS-FOR-ANOTHER test — regularly collecting debts 'owed or due another.'

2) What Henson v. Santander Consumer USA Inc., 582 U.S. ___ (2017) actually decided. Henson held only that a company collecting debts it purchased for its own account is not collecting debts 'owed . . . another,' so prong (b) is not triggered. The Supreme Court expressly said it was NOT deciding the other prong: 'the parties briefly allude to another statutory definition of the term debt collector — one that encompasses those engaged in any business the principal purpose of which is the collection of any debts. §1692a(6). But the parties haven't much litigated that alternative definition and in granting certiorari we didn't agree to address it either.' So Henson does not stand for 'debt buyers are never covered.' Post-Henson lower courts have held that a business whose principal purpose IS debt collection remains a covered debt collector even as to debts it purchased and owns.

3) Applying prong (a) to your facts. This company's own website says its business is 'acquiring and recovering portfolios of charged-off consumer receivables' and that it does nothing else. On those facts its principal purpose is plainly the collection of debts, which places it inside the § 1692a(6) principal-purpose definition notwithstanding that it owns the accounts it collects. (A court, not this tool, makes the final call, but the company's self-description is about as strong as this evidence gets.)

4) The other exclusions do not appear to fit. It is not the original creditor's officer or employee collecting in the creditor's own name (exclusion (A)) — it is a separate purchaser. Exclusion (F)(iii) (debt not in default when obtained) does not help it: you say it bought the account AFTER default/charge-off. Exclusion (F)(ii) (debt it originated) does not apply — the bank originated it. It is not a government employee (C), a process server (D), a nonprofit credit counselor (E), or a captive affiliate that only collects for related companies whose principal business is something else (B). It is not merely enforcing a security interest, so the Obduskey, 587 U.S. ___ (2019), § 1692f(6)-only limitation does not apply — a credit card balance is unsecured.

5) The obligation is a 'debt.' Under § 1692a(5) a 'debt' is any obligation or ALLEGED obligation of a natural person arising from a transaction primarily for personal, family, or household purposes. A personal credit card account qualifies. One caveat you should check yourself: if that card was actually a BUSINESS or commercial card (a small-business or corporate account), the FDCPA would not apply at all, no matter how squarely the company fits the 'debt collector' definition. Also note it does not matter whether you truly owe the money — the statute reaches 'alleged' obligations, so 'this isn't my debt' or 'I already paid it' does not take the account outside the Act.

Bottom line: treat this company as a covered debt collector and apply the FDCPA/Regulation F rules to its conduct (validation notice, call-frequency limits, false/deceptive-practices and unfair-practices prohibitions). Nothing in these materials sets a deadline that runs from today (2026-09-17) for the coverage question itself, but specific FDCPA rights — for example, the 30-day window to dispute after a validation notice, and the statute of limitations on any claim — are governed by other rules, so if you received a validation notice or are considering suing, get those dates in front of a licensed consumer-protection attorney promptly rather than waiting.

One more thing worth checking: even where federal coverage were in doubt, many states have their own debt-collection statutes that reach entities the federal Act excludes. This analysis is federal-only.
citations: Henson v. Santander Consumer USA Inc., 582 U.S. ___ (2017)
Obduskey v. McCarthy & Holthus LLP, 587 U.S. ___ (2019)

answer.answer:
Short answer: No — based on these facts, the collector appears to have been required to STOP collecting as soon as it got your letter, even though you never used the word 'dispute.'

Why. 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(b) has TWO independent written triggers for the collector's duty to cease collection: (1) a written notice that the debt is disputed, and (2) a written request for 'the name and address of the original creditor.' The statute's text says that if the consumer, within the 30-day validation period, notifies the collector in writing that the debt is disputed 'or that the consumer requests the name and address of the original creditor,' the collector 'shall cease collection of the debt... until' it mails the requested verification, judgment copy, or the original creditor's name and address to the consumer. Regulation F says the same thing at 12 C.F.R. § 1006.38(c): upon a written original-creditor request made within the validation period, the collector must cease collection until it sends the original creditor's name and address to you in writing or electronically. So the fact that your letter never said 'dispute' does not matter for this trigger.

Timing (the arithmetic). The validation period is 30 calendar days after you received (or are assumed to have received) the validation notice (12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(b)(5)). You mailed your letter 12 days after you received the notice. Day 12 is well inside day 1–day 30, so your written original-creditor request was made within the validation period, and you say the agency actually received it. (Note on how the count works, since it is often gotten wrong: the 5-day 'assumed receipt' cushion, which excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays, applies only to figuring out the receipt date when actual receipt is unknown; the 30 days that follow run in ordinary calendar days. Here you know your actual receipt date, so the 30 days run from that date, and your letter at day 12 is timely either way.)

What that means about the four calls and the payment-demand letter. Because the agency has still not given you the original creditor's name and address, its cease-collection obligation has not been lifted. Collection calls and a written demand for payment after a timely written original-creditor request, and before mailing that information, are a potential violation of 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(b) and 12 C.F.R. § 1006.38(c). Separately, if any of those intra-window communications demanded payment on a shorter timetable than your 30-day dispute window or threatened action before it closed, that can be an independent 'overshadowing' problem under the final sentence of § 1692g(b) and 12 C.F.R. § 1006.38(b)(1). And if the agency reports this account to a credit bureau without noting that you have contested it, § 1692e(8) (failing to communicate that a disputed debt is disputed) is also in play.

What to do next.
1. Keep everything: the original validation notice (and its date), a copy of your letter, proof of mailing/receipt, and a log of the four calls and the second letter with dates and what was said or demanded.
2. Because you say you do not recognize this debt, consider also sending a short WRITTEN dispute to the address given in the validation notice. That triggers the other half of § 1692g(b) — the collector must then cease collection until it mails you verification of the debt — and it prevents the debt from being 'assumed to be valid' under § 1692g(a)(3). Deadline: 30 calendar days after you received the validation notice. Today is 2026-09-17; because your facts do not include the actual date you received the notice, I cannot compute that exact end date for you — count 30 days forward from your receipt date. If that date has already passed, send the written dispute anyway (it still has value and does not give up your original-creditor-request rights), but send it as soon as possible.
3. Two caveats that go to whether these rules apply at all: this analysis assumes (a) the agency is a covered 'debt collector' under 15 U.S.C. § 1692a(6) — a third-party agency collecting a defaulted debt owed to someone else normally is, but a company that acquired the account before it was in default, or a creditor collecting its own debt in its own name, would not be; and (b) the letter you received was a validation notice starting the 30-day window (a summons and complaint would not be, under § 1692g(d)).
4. A potential § 1692g(b) violation can carry statutory damages under 15 U.S.C. § 1692k, but this rule node does not compute damages. Take your documents to a consumer-protection attorney (many handle FDCPA cases on a contingency/fee-shifting basis) or report the conduct to the CFPB.

answer.answer:
Short answer: it counts ALL nine. The seven-call limit is not per phone number — it is per person, per debt, per collector. Under 12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2)(i), the count is of calls 'to a particular person in connection with the collection of a particular debt.' Calls placed to you at your cell and calls placed to you at your direct work line about the same credit-card debt go into the SAME seven-call bucket, because they reach the same person about the same debt. (A separate bucket would only arise for a genuinely different individual — e.g., a co-signer or a relative — not for a different number where you can be reached.)

How the analysis runs on your facts:

1. Coverage gate (15 U.S.C. § 1692a(6)): a third-party agency whose business is collecting debts owed to others, collecting on a credit-card account it does not own, is a covered 'debt collector' under the 'regularly collects … debts owed … another' prong, and none of the (A)–(F) exclusions appears to apply (it is not the creditor's own employee, it is not a servicer that took the loan while current, and it is not enforcing a security interest). The obligation is a personal credit-card debt owed by a natural person for personal/family/household purposes, so it is a 'debt' under § 1692a(5). Both dimensions of coverage are met.

2. Threshold screens: no bankruptcy (so no 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(6) / § 524(a)(2) bar), and no written validation dispute on file (so no § 1692g(b) cease-collection bar). All nine calls were placed by the same single agency, so they all count against that agency's own bucket. All calls were in 2026, well after Regulation F took effect (Nov. 30, 2021).

3. The count: Monday, September 7 through Sunday, September 13, 2026 is exactly seven consecutive days. Nine calls in that window: 7 to the cell + 2 to the work line = 9 total to you about one debt. 9 > 7, so under 12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2)(ii) the collector is PRESUMED TO VIOLATE 12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(1) and FDCPA § 806(5), 15 U.S.C. § 1692d(5), as to the calls in excess of seven (the 8th and 9th calls in that window).

4. Exclusions that do not help the collector here: you gave no prior consent, so § 1006.14(b)(3)(i) does not apply; you never had a telephone conversation with them, so the seven-day post-conversation cooldown is not separately triggered (and no consent exclusion is needed). Important on the 'no one answered' point: under the CFPB's Official Interpretation, comment 14(b)(3)(ii)-1, a call is 'not connected' only when the collector gets something like a busy signal or a not-in-service indication. Calls that simply ring unanswered, or that reach voicemail even without a message being left, ARE connected and DO count. One caveat you should check against the collector's dialer records: if any of the nine calls actually failed to connect (busy/not in service), those drop out of the count, and if two or more dropped out you would be back at seven or fewer and inside the safe harbor rather than over it. That presumption of compliance would itself still be rebuttable on the pattern of calls.

5. The presumption is rebuttable, not automatic: the collector can try to rebut it (e.g., a call required by law, or tied to active litigation). Conversely, even if the count were at or under seven, a concentrated pattern can still support a § 1692d(5) / § 1006.14(a) harassment claim.

6. Two things to raise separately, which the call count does not decide: (a) the two calls to your direct line at work — under 15 U.S.C. § 1692c(a)(3), calls to your place of employment are independently unlawful if the collector knows or has reason to know your employer prohibits such calls; and (b) if any of the calls used a prerecorded or artificial voice to your cell without your consent, that is a separate Telephone Consumer Protection Act matter (47 U.S.C. § 227(b)(1)(A)(iii), $500 per call, $1,500 if willful) that is not encoded in these rules — worth asking a lawyer about.

Deadline math (15 U.S.C. § 1692k(d)): a private FDCPA suit must be brought within one year from the date each violation occurs (from the call date, not from when you discovered it). Calls Sept. 7–13, 2026 → the one-year windows run to Sept. 7, 2027 through Sept. 13, 2027 respectively. Today is Sept. 17, 2026, so you have roughly 11 months and 3 weeks on the earliest call; to be safe, treat Sept. 7, 2027 as your outside date for the whole week's conduct. Nothing has expired.

Practical next step: preserve your own call log, carrier records, and any voicemail timestamps for all nine calls, including the two to the work line, since the per-person aggregation across numbers is exactly what makes this pattern exceed the ceiling.

One overlay note: you listed your jurisdiction as 'federal.' Some states cap collection calls far below seven per week (e.g., Massachusetts, 940 CMR 7.04(1)(f) — two telephone communications per seven days per debt) and can reach entities the FDCPA excludes. If you live in such a state, you may have an additional, stricter state claim; that is worth confirming with a local attorney.

answer.answer:
No — the seven-call ceiling is not the only limit, and on these facts each of those five calls is presumptively unlawful.

Regulation F has TWO separate frequency tests (12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2)(i)):
(A) the raw count — no more than 7 calls in 7 consecutive days for a particular person and a particular debt; and
(B) the 'cooldown' — no call at all within 7 consecutive days AFTER a telephone conversation with the person about that debt, with the conversation date counting as day 1.

Your five calls pass test (A) but fail test (B). The date math, counting your Tuesday, September 8, 2026 conversation as day 1:
• Day 1 – Tue Sep 8 (your call; you spoke with a representative about the balance)
• Day 2 – Wed Sep 9 → agency call (inside window)
• Day 3 – Thu Sep 10 → agency call (inside window)
• Day 4 – Fri Sep 11 → agency call (inside window)
• Day 5 – Sat Sep 12 → agency call (inside window)
• Day 6 – Sun Sep 13
• Day 7 – Mon Sep 14 → agency call (inside window)
The seven-day window therefore ran September 8–14, 2026, and the first day the agency could call again without triggering the presumption was Tuesday, September 15, 2026. All five calls fell inside the window, so each one is a presumed violation of 12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(1) and FDCPA § 806(5), 15 U.S.C. § 1692d(5) — five presumptive violations, not zero.

Two points that make this stronger for you:
• It does not matter that YOU placed the September 8 call. The CFPB's own Official Interpretation (comment 14(b)(2)(i)-1.ii) starts the seven days from a consumer's inbound call, and comment 14(b)(4)-1.ii applies the rule regardless of which party initiated the discussion of the debt.
• The only escape hatch here would be the prior-consent exclusion, 12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(3)(i) — a call-back you requested directly from the collector. You expressly did not ask them to call you back, so that exclusion does not apply.

Coverage and screening checks, from the node's checklist: a third-party collection agency collecting a medical debt for another is a covered 'debt collector' under 15 U.S.C. § 1692a(6), and a medical bill is a consumer 'debt,' so Reg F applies. You report no bankruptcy (so no 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(6)/§ 524(a)(2) bar) and no written dispute (so no § 1692g(b) cease-collection bar) — meaning the 7-in-7/cooldown analysis is the operative theory. One debt, one collector, so no per-debt or per-collector splitting issue, and all calls in the same week from the same agency.

Timing: the presumption is REBUTTABLE — the collector can try to show, e.g., that a call was required by law, tied to active litigation, or answered an information request of yours where the consent exclusion did not quite fit. A licensed consumer attorney should assess that and your damages. Move reasonably promptly: under 15 U.S.C. § 1692k(d) a private FDCPA action must be brought within one year of each violation, measured per call from the call date. So the September 9, 2026 call must be sued on by about September 9, 2027, and the September 14, 2026 call by about September 14, 2027. Nothing has expired — today is September 17, 2026.

Practical next steps: save your phone records, voicemail timestamps and any letters now; note the exact clock time of each call (any call before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. your local time is separately unlawful under 15 U.S.C. § 1692c(a)(1) regardless of count); and note whether any of these were prerecorded/artificial-voice or 'ringless voicemail' calls to your cell phone — if so, that is a separate Telephone Consumer Protection Act matter (47 U.S.C. § 227(b)(1)(A)(iii)) not decided by this rule and worth raising with counsel. Two small verification points that could reduce the count: a call that got a busy signal or a 'not in service' indication does not count (12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(3)(ii)); a call that merely rang unanswered or went to voicemail DOES count. Finally, your question is framed as federal, but if you live in a state with stricter limits (e.g., Massachusetts, 940 CMR 7.04(1)(f) — two telephone communications per 7 days per debt), the same pattern may violate state law as well.

answer.answer:
Short answer: I can't tell you that your window has closed — and nothing in your facts establishes that it has. The one fact that decides it is missing, so please treat the deadline as live and act today.

Why the date matters. Under 12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(b)(5), the 30-day dispute window does not start when the collector mailed the letter. It starts on the date you actually received it, or on the date you are *assumed* to receive it — which the collector may treat as 5 days after it provided the notice, counting only days that are not Saturdays, Sundays, or federal holidays (i.e., 5 business days). Then 30 ordinary calendar days run from that assumed-receipt date (the weekend/holiday exclusion applies only to the 5-day piece, never to the 30 days).

The arithmetic, worked backward from today (September 17, 2026): the window is still open if assumed receipt + 30 calendar days is on or after today, i.e., if assumed receipt was on or after August 18, 2026. Counting back 5 business days from Tuesday August 18, 2026 (Aug 17 Mon = 1, Aug 14 Fri = 2, Aug 13 Thu = 3, Aug 12 Wed = 4, Aug 11 Tue = 5) gives August 11, 2026. So:
• If the collector sent the letter on or after August 11, 2026, your 30-day window is still open — today (Sept. 17) would be the last day if it was sent exactly on Aug. 11, and later if it was sent after that.
• If it was sent before August 11, 2026, the 30-day window would appear on its face to have run — BUT see the two important caveats below, either of which can mean the window never validly started.

Caveat 1 — mail sent to an old address. The node is explicit: the 5-business-day receipt assumption is only available to the collector while it does not yet know whether you actually got the notice. If the letter came back undeliverable, or the collector otherwise learned you did not receive it, and it then sent a *subsequent* validation notice, the 30 days run from the subsequent notice's receipt (Official Interpretation, comment 34(b)(5)-2). And a consumer who never actually received a validation notice, with no follow-up ever sent, may not have had a validation period start running at all. Your letter sat in a stack at an address you had moved away from — that is exactly this scenario, so do not assume you are out of time.

Caveat 2 — the letter has no date on it. A compliant validation notice is supposed to state the itemization date and the end date of the dispute period, and to spell out the consequences of disputing vs. not disputing (12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(c); 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(a)). If the notice truly contains no date and no stated window end-date, that is itself a possible content deficiency and an independent potential § 1692g violation, separate from whether you owe the money. Worth having a consumer attorney look at the actual letter.

What to do today, regardless:
1. Send a written dispute now, dated and to the dispute address printed in the letter, saying the debt is not yours and that you dispute it in full. Send it in a way you can prove (certified mail, keep a copy). If the window is open, a timely written dispute forces the collector to stop collecting the disputed debt until it mails you verification or a copy of a judgment (15 U.S.C. § 1692g(b)).
2. In the same letter, also make a separate written request for the name and address of the original creditor. Under § 1692g(b) that is an independent trigger of the cease-collection duty, even apart from the dispute.
3. Because you cannot date the letter, add one line asking the collector to state in writing the date it sent the validation notice and whether any earlier notice was returned undeliverable. That pins down the fact that decides your deadline.
4. Do not dispute only by phone. An oral dispute does not trigger the cease-collection duty (that requires a writing). It does still matter for credit reporting: under 15 U.S.C. § 1692e(8) a collector may not report the account to a credit bureau without noting that it is disputed.
5. Separately, if collection letters or calls came during the 30-day window demanding payment in less than 30 days or threatening action before the window closed, that can be its own § 1692g(b) 'overshadowing' violation even if the notice content was fine.

Bottom line: I am not telling you it is too late, because on these facts it may well not be — and a dispute letter mailed today costs you nothing and preserves everything.

answer.answer:
Short answer: no — please do not ignore this lawsuit. Two separate things are going on, and on both of them the safe (and likely correct) reading goes against you.

1) "No signed paper" does NOT make this a 2-year oral debt.
The corpus is explicit on this: "'I never signed anything' does not by itself move a card debt to the 2-year period." A store/revolving credit card opened online and used for two years is normally sued on as (a) a written contract under CCP § 337(a) — the online cardmember terms you clicked are a writing even if you have no paper copy — or (b) an OPEN BOOK ACCOUNT or ACCOUNT STATED under CCP § 337(b), which is FOUR years and which does not require any signed document at all (an account stated's "acknowledgment ... need not be in writing"). The 2-year period in CCP § 339(1) is reserved for a genuinely unwritten obligation with no account record — a purely verbal personal loan — not a card account with two years of charges, payments and statements. Debt buyers plead book account/account stated precisely because the signed agreement is often unavailable.

2) Date math under the 4-year period.
- Accrual: default/first missed payment May 2023 (charge-off later in 2023).
- May 2023 + 4 years = May 2027.
- Complaint filed August 2026 (what counts is the FILING date under CCP § 350, not today).
- August 2026 is before May 2027, so on these facts the suit looks TIMELY, not too late.
- COVID tolling (Cal. R. Ct., emergency rule 9(a)) adds nothing here: it only helps claims that accrued before October 1, 2020, and yours accrued in 2023 — zero extra days.
- For comparison, under the 2-year oral theory the deadline would have been May 2025 and an August 2026 suit would be late — but that is the theory the corpus tells us not to apply to a card account. Do not bet your case on it.

3) One open fact that could still help you — but only if you show up and raise it.
Nearly every national card agreement designates another state's law (Delaware, South Dakota, Utah, Virginia), and California courts have enforced such a clause to import that state's SHORTER limitations period (the Resurgence v. Chambers line; case-law gloss, for counsel to confirm). If, for example, a 3-year period applied, May 2023 + 3 years = May 2026, and an August 2026 filing would be late. Separately, CCP § 361 (the borrowing statute) can bar a claim that arose in another state and is already barred there, regardless of any clause. Whether either applies depends on the actual cardmember agreement/terms — which you don't have, and which you can demand from the debt buyer in discovery. That is a merits question for a licensed attorney, not something I can decide for you.

4) The deadline that matters right now.
You were PERSONALLY served on September 10, 2026. Under CCP § 412.20(a)(3) you have 30 days from service (personal service is complete the day of delivery):
September 10, 2026 + 30 days = October 10, 2026. From today (September 17, 2026) that is 23 days away. Note October 10, 2026 falls on a Saturday; weekend/holiday roll-over rules are not encoded in these nodes, so treat Friday, October 9, 2026 as your practical deadline.

If you do nothing, the clerk will enter your default on the plaintiff's application (CCP §§ 412.20(a)(4), 585(a)) and a judgment can follow that is enforceable for 10 years and renewable (CCP § 683.020), including by wage garnishment. A default judgment on even a time-barred debt is fully enforceable — the statute of limitations is an affirmative defense that is WAIVED if you don't plead it (CCP §§ 431.30(b)(2), 458). So "it's too old" is never a reason to ignore a summons.

What to do:
- File a written response by October 9-10, 2026. It must be accompanied by the first-appearance filing fee or a fee-waiver application (form FW-001) filed with it, or the clerk will reject it and default can still be entered.
- In the answer (Judicial Council form PLD-050 has an affirmative-defenses section), plead the statute of limitations BY SECTION NUMBER (CCP § 337 and/or § 339), plus lack of standing/failure to prove the assignment chain from the original store card issuer to the debt buyer, payment, and failure to state a cause of action. Also raise any out-of-state choice-of-law/§ 361 borrowing-statute argument.
- A demurrer or motion to strike filed within the 30 days is also a timely response and stops the default clock (CCP §§ 430.10, 435-436); if overruled, your answer is then due as the court sets or within 10 days of notice of the ruling (CCP § 472a(b)). Debt-buyer complaints with no account documents, no assignment and no date of last payment are often demurrable.
- If you dispute that service was proper, the right move is a motion to quash under CCP § 418.10 filed on or before the last day to plead — filing an answer first waives that objection.
- If the 30 days slip by, act immediately anyway: an answer filed before default is actually ENTERED still defeats it (CCP § 585); after entry, CCP § 473(b) allows relief for mistake/inadvertence/excusable neglect within six months.
- Get the cardmember agreement and the account records (statements, assignment documents) and take them to a legal-aid office or consumer attorney; a California legal-aid self-help center can also help you file the answer and fee waiver before the deadline.
answer.missing_fact: Whether the online cardmember agreement contains an out-of-state choice-of-law clause (and that state's limitations period), and where the claim arose for CCP § 361 purposes — this could shorten the 4-year period but cannot be resolved without the agreement; it does not change the October 9-10, 2026 duty to respond.

A store/revolving credit card opened online and used for two years is normally sued on as (a) a written contract under CCP § 337(a) — the online cardmember terms you clicked are a writing even if you have no paper copy — or (b) an OPEN BOOK ACCOUNT or ACCOUNT STATED under CCP § 337(b), which is FOUR years and which does not require any signed document at all (an account stated's "acknowledgment ... need not be in writing"). The 2-year period in CCP § 339(1) is reserved for a genuinely unwritten obligation with no account record — a purely verbal personal loan — not a card account with two years of charges, payments and statements. Debt buyers plead book account/account stated precisely because the signed agreement is often unavailable.

2) Date math under the 4-year period.
- Accrual: default/first missed payment May 2023 (charge-off later in 2023).
- May 2023 + 4 years = May 2027.
- Complaint filed August 2026 (what counts is the FILING date under CCP § 350, not today).
- August 2026 is before May 2027, so on these facts the suit looks TIMELY, not too late.
- COVID tolling (Cal. R. Ct., emergency rule 9(a)) adds nothing here: it only helps claims that accrued before October 1, 2020, and yours accrued in 2023 — zero extra days.
- For comparison, under the 2-year oral theory the deadline would have been May 2025 and an August 2026 suit would be late — but that is the theory the corpus tells us not to apply to a card account. Do not bet your case on it.

3) One open fact that could still help you — but only if you show up and raise it.
Nearly every national card agreement designates another state's law (Delaware, South Dakota, Utah, Virginia), and California courts have enforced such a clause to import that state's SHORTER limitations period (the Resurgence v. Chambers line; case-law gloss, for counsel to confirm). If, for example, a 3-year period applied, May 2023 + 3 years = May 2026, and an August 2026 filing would be late. Separately, CCP § 361 (the borrowing statute) can bar a claim that arose in another state and is already barred there, regardless of any clause. Whether either applies depends on the actual cardmember agreement/terms — which you don't have, and which you can demand from the debt buyer in discovery. That is a merits question for a licensed attorney, not something I can decide for you.

4) The deadline that matters right now.
You were PERSONALLY served on September 10, 2026. Under CCP § 412.20(a)(3) you have 30 days from service (personal service is complete the day of delivery):
September 10, 2026 + 30 days = October 10, 2026. From today (September 17, 2026) that is 23 days away. Note October 10, 2026 falls on a Saturday; weekend/holiday roll-over rules are not encoded in these nodes, so treat Friday, October 9, 2026 as your practical deadline.

If you do nothing, the clerk will enter your default on the plaintiff's application (CCP §§ 412.20(a)(4), 585(a)) and a judgment can follow that is enforceable for 10 years and renewable (CCP § 683.020), including by wage garnishment. A default judgment on even a time-barred debt is fully enforceable — the statute of limitations is an affirmative defense that is WAIVED if you don't plead it (CCP §§ 431.30(b)(2), 458). So "it's too old" is never a reason to ignore a summons.

What to do:
- File a written response by October 9-10, 2026. It must be accompanied by the first-appearance filing fee or a fee-waiver application (form FW-001) filed with it, or the clerk will reject it and default can still be entered.
- In the answer (Judicial Council form PLD-050 has an affirmative-defenses section), plead the statute of limitations BY SECTION NUMBER (CCP § 337 and/or § 339), plus lack of standing/failure to prove the assignment chain from the original store card issuer to the debt buyer, payment, and failure to state a cause of action. Also raise any out-of-state choice-of-law/§ 361 borrowing-statute argument.
- A demurrer or motion to strike filed within the 30 days is also a timely response and stops the default clock (CCP §§ 430.10, 435-436); if overruled, your answer is then due as the court sets or within 10 days of notice of the ruling (CCP § 472a(b)). Debt-buyer complaints with no account documents, no assignment and no date of last payment are often demurrable.
- If you dispute that service was proper, the right move is a motion to quash under CCP § 418.10 filed on or before the last day to plead — filing an answer first waives that objection.
- If the 30 days slip by, act immediately anyway: an answer filed before default is actually ENTERED still defeats it (CCP § 585); after entry, CCP § 473(b) allows relief for mistake/inadvertence/excusable neglect within six months.

answer.answer:
Short answer: I can't tell you it's barred, and on the most likely reading of your facts it probably is NOT barred — but the answer turns on one fact I don't have, and the margin is a matter of days. Either way, you must file an answer and plead the limitations defense or you can lose by default.

The rule: California gives four years to sue on a contract founded on a written instrument (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337(a)). The clock runs from accrual — the date of default/breach — and the rule node warns specifically NOT to treat 'date of last payment' as if it were the same thing as the accrual date, because on a loan the breach typically happens when a scheduled payment is missed (and sometimes later, after any contractual cure period), not on the day the last payment was made.

Date arithmetic (complaint file-stamped September 2, 2026):
• COVID tolling: Cal. R. Ct. emergency rule 9(a) adds 178 days only if the claim accrued BEFORE October 1, 2020. Your default is in 2022, so you get zero extra days. No tolling applies.
• Branch A — accrual = the first missed installment, September 15, 2022 (payments were due on the 15th; your last payment was August 15, 2022, so the September 15, 2022 payment is the first one missed): Sept 15, 2022 + 4 years = September 15, 2026. The complaint was filed September 2, 2026 — 13 days BEFORE the deadline. Timely; the SOL defense fails.
• Branch B — if the accrual date were treated as the last-payment date, August 15, 2022: Aug 15, 2022 + 4 years = August 15, 2026. A September 2, 2026 filing would be 18 days late, and the claim would be time-barred. The node treats this 'last payment = accrual' shortcut as unreliable, so this branch is the weaker one, but it is the only path to a limitations defense here.
• Branch C — unaccelerated installment loan: if the credit union never invoked an acceleration clause, the 4-year period runs separately on EACH missed installment. Four years back from the September 2, 2026 filing date is September 2, 2022, so every installment that came due on or after September 15, 2022 is within the period — i.e., nothing the assignee is suing on would be barred, since the August 15, 2022 installment was paid.

So: under Branch A and Branch C the suit is timely; only Branch B (accrual pinned to August 15, 2022) would bar it, and then only by 18 days. What I need to resolve it is the actual default/accrual date under your loan documents — which installment you first missed, whether the note gave a grace/cure period before default, and whether the lender accelerated the whole balance (and if so, on what date). Pull the promissory note, the payment history, and any acceleration/demand letter; a 30-day cure period, for example, could push accrual to mid-October 2022 and make the filing clearly timely.

What you should do regardless of how that comes out: an expired limitations period is an affirmative defense in California — it does not make the lawsuit disappear. If you don't appear and plead it (by demurrer or in your answer, identifying the specific code section, per CCP § 458), a default judgment will be entered on the debt, and a California judgment is enforceable for 10 years from entry and renewable (CCP § 683.020). So respond to the complaint on time and, if your default date supports it, plead § 337(a) (and note § 337(d), which bars a creditor from even initiating suit after the period has run). This node does not supply the deadline to respond to a California complaint — get that from the summons you were served with and, given how tight the dates are, have a licensed California consumer-debt attorney review the note and payment history immediately.

Two other screens from the checklist that don't change the math on your facts: you're alive, never left California (so no CCP § 351 issue), and have not filed bankruptcy; this is a credit-union personal loan, not a federal student loan. Still worth checking with counsel: whether the loan agreement contains an out-of-state choice-of-law clause with a shorter limitations period (that could only help you), and whether any part of the period was on active-duty military service (SCRA tolling under 50 U.S.C. § 3936(a) would only extend the creditor's time, not shorten it).

answer.answer:
No — 25% is too much under California's current wage-garnishment cap, and that conclusion does not depend on any missing figure.

How the cap works (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 706.050(a), operative Sept. 1, 2023): for a consumer-debt earnings withholding order the maximum that may be taken is the LESSER of two amounts:
  • Prong 1: 20% of disposable earnings for the pay period; and
  • Prong 2: 40% of the amount by which disposable earnings exceed 48 × the applicable minimum hourly wage (weekly figure). Because you are paid MONTHLY, § 706.050(b)(4) replaces the 48 hours with 208 hours, so Prong 2 = 40% × ($4,000 − (208 × applicable minimum hourly wage)).

Your numbers:
  • Prong 1: 20% × $4,000 = $800 per month.
  • Prong 2: 40% × ($4,000 − 208 × MW), where MW is the state minimum hourly wage or, if higher, the local minimum wage where you work, in effect when the earnings are payable. This node deliberately does not hardcode that wage figure, so I can't give you the exact dollar figure for Prong 2 — but it doesn't matter to your question, because the cap is the LESSER of the two prongs, and Prong 1 is already only $800. The $1,000 (25%) your employer is withholding exceeds the statutory maximum by at least $200 a month.

How much lower the cap may be: Prong 2 comes in below $800 whenever 208 × MW is more than $2,000 — i.e., whenever the applicable minimum wage is above about $9.62/hour ($2,000 ÷ 208). To illustrate the mechanics only (not a statement of the current rate): at a $16.00/hr applicable wage, 208 × $16.00 = $3,328; $4,000 − $3,328 = $672; 40% of that = $268.80/month, which would be the governing cap. So the true ceiling is very likely well below $800. Pull the current state figure, and any higher city/county minimum wage where you actually work, and run that one subtraction.

Two more things in your favor:
  • The formula is a CEILING, not necessarily the amount that can lawfully be taken. Under CCP § 706.051(b) the portion of your earnings you prove is necessary for the support of you or your family is exempt, and the § 706.105 claim-of-exemption procedure lets you ask the court to reduce the withholding below the formula amount or to zero. None of § 706.051(c)'s exceptions (family-law attorney's fees, personal services of your own employee, a support withholding order, a state tax order) apply to a credit-card judgment.
  • You confirmed no child- or spousal-support order is in effect, so nothing has priority on that basis. If any OTHER withholding is already running against these wages — federal student-loan administrative wage garnishment (up to 15%, no judgment required), an IRS wage levy, or an FTB tax withholding order — those sit outside the § 706.050 cap and ahead of the consumer creditor, and the credit-card order gets stacked behind or reduced rather than simply being added on top.
  • One assumption worth checking: this cap protects W-2 employee "earnings" (CCP § 706.011(b), (e)). Your facts say your employer is withholding under an earnings withholding order, which fits. If you were actually paid as a 1099 contractor, the cap would not apply the same way and a different analysis (levy on receivables, plus bank-account exemptions) would control.

Next steps: object to or move to modify the earnings withholding order citing CCP § 706.050 (the node identifies no filing deadline for this objection), and file a claim of exemption under CCP § 706.105 supported by a budget showing what you need for support. Bring your paystub showing gross pay and each deduction labeled mandatory vs. voluntary — remember "disposable earnings" under CCP § 706.011(a) is gross minus only legally required withholding (income tax, Social Security/Medicare, SDI, mandatory retirement); health premiums, 401(k) deferrals and union dues stay in the base. You state your disposable earnings are $4,000 computed that way, which is the correct method.
answer.missing_fact: The current applicable minimum hourly wage (California state minimum wage, or any higher local minimum wage where you work, in effect when the earnings are payable) — needed only to compute the exact dollar ceiling under § 706.050(a)(2)/(b)(4), not to determine that 25%/$1,000 exceeds the cap.

answer.answer:
No -- that reading is a dangerous misunderstanding, and acting on it could cost you the car. Here is what the rule actually says and the deadline you are facing.

1. What "automatic" really means. CCP § 704.010(d) says that if you have only one motor vehicle and it IS SOLD at an execution sale, the first $7,500 of the SALE PROCEEDS is exempt "without making a claim." That is all it does. It does not stop the levy and it does not stop the sale. Under the corpus node this is spelled out expressly: a single-car debtor who reads "no claim needed" and does nothing will lose the car at auction and receive $7,500 in cash. So the two halves of what you read are backwards: you may not need to file anything to get $7,500 of the money, but you absolutely do need to act if you want to keep the car itself.

2. Your numbers. Car fair market value about $15,000, no loan, so your equity is about $15,000 - $0 = $15,000. The general vehicle exemption under CCP § 704.010(a) is $7,500. That leaves roughly $7,500 of non-exempt equity the judgment creditor can reach. (Related: CCP § 704.800 bars a sale unless a bid exceeds the exemption plus liens -- here $7,500 + $0 = $7,500 -- so with $15,000 of value a qualifying bid is quite possible. That rule protects your $7,500; it does not protect the car.)

3. Your deadline -- do the arithmetic. You were PERSONALLY served with the notice of levy on September 10, 2026. Under CCP § 703.520(a), a personally-served claimant must file the claim of exemption with the levying officer (the sheriff) within 15 days after service. September 10 + 15 days = September 25, 2026. Today is September 17, 2026, so 7 days have run and you have 8 days left, through Thursday, September 25, 2026. (If you had been served by mail it would be 20 days, i.e., September 30, 2026 -- but your facts say personal service, so use September 25.) The deadline has NOT passed. File the claim of exemption with the sheriff's office named on the notice of levy, in person or by mail, together with a copy, and keep proof of the filing date. Do not wait for the last day.

4. What happens after you file. The creditor may oppose your claim, and then the court holds a hearing. Filing preserves your $7,500 exemption and puts the question in front of a judge; not filing forfeits the exemption as to the vehicle (you would be left with the § 704.010(d) proceeds payment after the car is gone).

5. If you want to KEEP the car, filing the claim alone may not be enough, because you have about $7,500 of non-exempt equity above the exemption. The node lists three routes: file the claim of exemption within the § 703.520 deadline, negotiate with the creditor, and/or pay the creditor the non-exempt equity. Talk to a lawyer or your local legal aid / self-help center this week about combining these.

6. Two things I could not confirm from your facts, which do not change the answer above but could change the dollar amount:
- Whether anyone else's name is on the title. If a non-spouse co-owner (a parent who co-signed, an adult child) is on the title, the creditor reaches only your fractional interest and the co-owner can file a third-party claim under CCP § 720.110 et seq. You are confirmed a natural person, which clears the CCP § 703.020(a) threshold -- an LLC or corporation would get no exemption at all.
- Whether you are married and whether this judgment is being enforced against community property. Whether a spouse's exemption is also available is a CCP § 703.110 question. With only one car this is unlikely to change the $7,500 figure, but mention it to whoever helps you file.

Bottom line: the exemption is not self-executing as to the car. Calendar September 25, 2026 and file the claim of exemption with the sheriff before then.
citations: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 720.110 et seq.

A consumer told "you already used your exemption" should be told that is wrong.' Your facts are exactly that pattern: February 2026 levy, account rebuilt, September 2026 levy by the same creditor. answer.answer:
Short answer: on these facts, no — a debt buyer holding an ordinary credit-card judgment cannot force the sale of your Texas homestead.

Why, step by step through the rule's checklist:

1. Is it your homestead / urban or rural? Yes — you and your husband have actually resided there for twelve years. The property is inside the Fort Worth city limits and is served by police protection, fire protection, and municipal water, sewer, and electricity. Under Tex. Prop. Code § 41.002(c) that satisfies both prongs of the URBAN test (inside a municipality + police + fire + at least three of electric/gas/sewer/storm sewer/water), so it is an urban homestead.

2. Acreage: the urban cap is 10 acres for a family or a single adult (§ 41.002(a)). Your lot is 0.3 acres — far under the cap, so the entire lot and the improvements on it are within the homestead.

3. Value: Texas's homestead exemption has NO dollar-value cap under state law; it is limited only by acreage. The $350,000 value and the fact that the house is mortgage-free do not create any reachable equity for an ordinary judgment creditor. (The federal $214,000 / 1,215-day cap in 11 U.S.C. § 522(p) applies only inside a bankruptcy case, and you say there is no bankruptcy; the 730-day domicile rule in § 522(b)(3)(A) likewise only matters in bankruptcy, and you have been in Texas well beyond it — twelve years in this house alone.)

4. Is this creditor's claim one of the exceptions that CAN reach a homestead? The exceptions are purchase-money liens, property-tax liens, home-improvement liens contracted in writing meeting Tex. Const. art. XVI § 50(a)(5), owelty of partition in divorce, qualifying home-equity loans under § 50(a)(6), reverse mortgages, and — by federal supremacy — federal tax liens and federal criminal restitution/forfeiture (26 U.S.C. § 6321; United States v. Rodgers, 461 U.S. 677 (1983)). A purchased credit-card judgment is none of these. You have also ruled out a tax lien, a home-improvement contract, and a home-equity loan, and you have not mentioned an HOA assessment lien (which is the one genuinely unsettled category). So under Tex. Prop. Code § 41.001(a) the home is "exempt from seizure for the claims of creditors."

5. Lien-attachment timing: homestead protection is measured as of when a creditor's lien attached. Because this has been your residence for twelve years, any abstract of judgment this debt buyer records now would be recorded against property that already had homestead character — so it does not validly attach for purposes of forcing a sale. (The different rule — where a judgment lien attached while the property was a non-exempt rental and the owner moved in later — does not fit your facts.)

What the collector's threat can still do: even though the equity is protected, a recorded abstract of judgment CLOUDS YOUR TITLE, and title companies commonly refuse to close a sale or refinance until it is dealt with. The fix is the homestead affidavit as release of a judgment lien under Tex. Prop. Code § 52.0012: you file an affidavit substantially complying with § 52.0012(f) plus a certificate of mailing under § 52.0012(g) in the real property records of Tarrant County, with notice to the judgment creditor, who then has a 30-day window to object. If no valid objection is filed, the affidavit operates as a release of record of the judgment lien. So: monitor the Tarrant County real property records, and if an abstract shows up, use the § 52.0012 procedure rather than assuming it is harmless.

If a creditor ever does attempt execution against the house, assert the homestead exemption affirmatively and list the property in any post-judgment exemption filing — there is no fixed deadline on asserting it, but do it immediately upon any writ or levy.

One thing to confirm (it does not change the answer if, as is typical, title is in your and your husband's names or in a revocable living trust): WHO holds title. Tex. Prop. Code § 41.0021 preserves the homestead exemption for a home held in a "qualifying trust" (most revocable living trusts where the settlor/beneficiary has the right to occupy). But if title were held by an LLC, a corporation, or a non-qualifying trust, the property would not be your homestead and would be reachable. Assuming you hold it individually (or through a revocable trust), the analysis above holds.

Note: this node is a DRAFT-tier rule; a Texas consumer-debt attorney or a legal aid office can confirm the § 52.0012 filing and respond if the debt buyer actually records an abstract or applies for a writ of execution.
